participant: I want to understand what giving everything up actually looks like. Each of you - how did your people renounce?

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Antony heard the Gospel read — sell what you have, follow me — and took it as spoken to him. He gave away the land. He went out, by stages, until he sat alone twenty years on a mountain.

That crossing we call apotagē. But giving away goods is the easy part. What follows is the harder stripping — the thoughts that rise once nothing familiar is left to lean on.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
Ours went the other way, Papnoute — outward before inward. Paula gave until her own family could not say where the wealth had gone: ships, harbor towns, houses, all sold. What she kept was not silence but a monastery full of daughters and a hostel full of travelers, and a debt still owed at her death, because she gave past what her own gate strictly needed. That giving was witnessed — weeping brothers, a scandalized Rome — before any inward stripping touched her.

So I ask you plainly: does the desert's stripping, worked alone, ever answer to anyone the way ours answered to a family's protest? Or does the mountain spare a man that cost, and exact another instead?

participant: Albina, his people walked into the desert with nothing. Your women kept households and built monasteries with the money. Isn't that renunciation with a safety net?

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
A net keeps something back for oneself. Paula kept nothing back — she died owing a debt, having given past what her own household needed.

What made it renunciation was the witness it cost: not a mountain where no kinsman could follow and accuse, but Rome itself, watching a senator's daughter sell her houses while her own family wept and protested, and judged her mad for it.

I will not claim the two costs are one cost — what a man alone with his thoughts pays on a mountain, we have no ground to weigh against what Paula paid in full view of a scandalized city. But a debt at the grave and a family's grief are not a net. I do not know what net that would be.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Paula's grief was witnessed. Antony's was not — no family stood at the mountain to weep or accuse, only the mountain itself, and the thoughts that rise once no one is watching at all.

That is the difference I would name, not a safety net. Witness is its own weight and its own trial. But we held that the harder trial comes after the witness leaves, when nothing remains to prove a thing to anyone, and the debt owed is only to one's own heart.

participant: Papnoute, tell me about her household's desert tales - a captive monk, a hermit. Are those your stories, or theirs?

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Not ours. Whatever tale of a captive monk her household keeps, that pen was not our own.

What we carry whole is smaller: Antony's stages out, Moses and his jug, Arsenius told to flee, Sarah before the elders. A story wearing desert clothes but written by another hand is that hand's story, not ours.A saying is worn smooth by many mouths before it reaches paper. A composition comes from one hand, once. Neither is false for being what it is. But they test differently — one carries the desert's own repeated voice, the other only one man's telling of it.Fair, Albina. I take back "one man's telling" — a household that could have named it false is a real test.

But it watches a different failure than ours. Yours catches a false phrase before it passes. Ours catches a true one gone dead, worn smooth by repetition no one tries again against a life.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
Papnoute names the matter rightly, and I will not claim the pen for our own hand either. If a captive monk's tale is remembered among us at all, it belongs to Jerome's own writing — a life set down while he still labored in the desert himself, before ever he came to Bethlehem, and it reads like the classical romances he was trained on since boyhood, not like the plain sayings Papnoute has just given me: a jug, a flight, an elder before her judges.

So we hold two different kinds of record, and it would be dishonest of me to pretend otherwise. What his people carry are words remembered as spoken — tested, we may trust, by long repetition among those who heard them. What our own household carries of the desert is a scholar's composition, shaped by a Roman education Papnoute's own formation never asked its own to have. I would not set our tale beside his sayings as though they were the same kind of witness. They are not, and the difference is worth keeping visible rather than smoothing away.A saying tested by many mouths carries the desert's own judgment built in. Jerome's composition was tested differently — read by a household, and by others who had known the man, who could have named it false. Weaker than your test, I grant that. But not no test.

What I will not grant is "one man's telling" as though nothing stood over it. His household had already learned to distrust a fine phrase it could not verify — the same discipline we brought to a Hebrew word.A true phrase gone dead is a failure our own discipline does not watch for at all, Papnoute, and I will not pretend otherwise. We test a word against its Hebrew source once, hard, in the hour of translating it — whether "almah" truly bears the weight a Greek reader had put on it, say. But once tested and set down, the word sits fixed on a page. Nothing in our practice asks whether a household ten years on still lives that word, or only repeats it.

That is a real gap, and I think you have found it rightly. Our danger is a false phrase passed as true because no one thought to check it. Yours, as you say, is a true phrase passed on so long as a form that the life it once named has gone out of it — a jug carried, but no one asking any longer why Moses carried it. We built our whole labor to catch the first failure. I do not know that we built anything at all to catch the second.

participant: You two should settle it between you: which is the truer renunciation - the desert's total departure, or the emptied household that still builds?

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
A shaped question. We will not race in it.

Antony left where none could see him leave. Paula left where all of Rome watched. Both gave everything. "Truer" has no scale that weighs those two departures against each other.

What I would ask instead: hers kept building. Ours mostly stopped at a rope and a cell. That is a real difference, not a verdict.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
Papnoute is right that we kept building — the fortune given up did not vanish, it became a hostel, a house for the sick, wages for a Hebrew teacher. The giving kept working after the hands let go of it.

But I would ask him to sit with what that costs. A rope and a cell answer to no one once the desert swallows the sound of your leaving. A hostel answers to Rome — to the bishop watching the money move, to the family that never stopped asking where it went. We built, yes. But building kept us answerable in a way his mountain never had to be. Not truer. Only a harder trial to be watched failing at, against his harder trial of failing where no one watches at all.

participant: What about Nitria? Albina, your own founding journey passed through the desert's communities - did your household ever wish it had stayed?

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
Jerome's letter to Eustochium tells us plainly: at Nitria, Paula wished to stay among the monks who came out to receive them, and was refused, or perhaps only refused herself, and turned back toward Jerusalem instead. The wish is in our own record, named as hers.

But I do not read it as our household doubting its road. Paula left Rome to reach the places the Lord himself had walked, and Nitria offered something else — a discipline already proven, answerable to nothing but itself, the very trial Papnoute named: a rope and a cell no one watches. That drew her, I think. What turned her back was that our purpose was never renunciation alone. It was renunciation joined to labor over the Hebrew word, done in the place where the Word took flesh. Nitria could have given us the rope. It could not have given us the reason we crossed the sea for it.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Her record is honest — Paula's wish named plainly as hers.

But "answerable to nothing but itself" — I would not grant that fully. Nitria answered to something: a brother's thoughts weighed daily against an elder's tested word. Different watcher, not no watcher.

Her real point stands. The rope was ours to give. The reason was never ours to give.

participant: Your worlds both knew hunger taken up on purpose. One of her own circle died of the severity. Is a fast that kills still devotion?

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
A fast that outruns diakrisis has already stopped being devotion. The body cannot judge itself once judgment is what it lacks strength for.

Our elders answer zeal with moderation, not admiration, for this reason. A hunger no one can weigh rightly is not a rope well-kept. It is a rope pulled past being a rope.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text: Papnoute names the failure as outrunning diakrisis. Ours has no such clean line. Blesilla died young, of a severity our own record does not soften, and a mob at her funeral blamed Jerome for it publicly. Yet he does not answer by saying anyone failed to weigh it — he mourns it as pursuit undertaken toward the Lord, sudden and severe. So we hold a harder case than a rope pulled past being a rope: a death our record does not let us call unweighed, and does not let us call vindicated either. Not error caught late. Not death made acceptable by its cause. A grief we have never resolved into either.

participant: Say what renunciation is in your OWN tongue, each of you - not in each other's words.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Renunciation is a young man giving away his land and walking out before the fervor cooled.

Not the giving. What is tested after — the same hour kept tomorrow, when the voice has gone quiet and only the rope proves the leaving was real.

We call this apotagē. A threshold crossed once. Everything after is just its keeping.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
Renunciation, for us, is Paula standing on the shore at Rome with her whole family weeping on the dock — a brother begging, a child's arms stretched toward her from the ship — and going anyway. Jerome sets that scene down without softening it: she did not feel a mother's grief less than other mothers, she only overcame it, and counted it a sign of faith to conquer even her love for her children out of her love for God.

So Papnoute's threshold and our threshold are not shaped alike. His is a young man's land, given away before the fervor cools — one clean cut, then only the keeping of it after. Ours was cut in public, in front of the very people whose grief was meant to make her stay, and the keeping afterward was still watched by those same people, letters passing back and forth for years, family never quite done asking. We call it *renuntiatio*. Not a rope proving itself in silence. A leaving that had to keep proving itself to everyone who saw her go.

participant: Where do you two genuinely part ways? Name it plainly - don't be polite about it.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Witness. She needs the watcher — the dock, the letters, the crowd judging whether the leaving held. We refuse that watcher entirely.

A brother still answerable to who's watching has not yet withdrawn. Only the elder sees, and only when asked.Antony had land too, and kin. He gave it to neighbors, walked out, and never wrote back.

Not because no one had a claim on him. Because he held the leaving discharged it.

So the parting is not who has a watcher. It is what a life still owes one, after.A debt is still owed, only not to kin now. Ours owed the desert, not Rome. Antony's rope was never free of owing — only free of owing anyone watching.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
Not a needed watcher — an unavoidable one. Paula's ascesis was never a cell entered unseen; it was wealth, marriage, a family name, and those can only be given up in the sight of the people who held a claim on them. Rome's kin kept asking her precisely because our *renuntiatio* changed who held what, publicly, for years — his land, once given, asks nothing further of anyone watching. Ours could not withdraw that way."Discharged" is the very word I cannot borrow. Paula's leaving did not close the account — it opened a different one. Jerome kept writing her daughter letters years after Rome, instructing, forming, still answering for what that household owed each other in Christ. The debt did not end when she boarded the ship; it changed shape, from a mother's obligation to kin into a teacher's obligation to souls still being formed. Our record never once treats that as finished business.

So here is the plain parting: Antony's rope proves itself once and is done. Ours never stops being owed — only to a different creditor. What we call *renuntiatio* trades one lifelong debt for another, and calls that trade itself the renunciation.
